claim: Male infertility affects more than 6% of males globally.
source: Male infertility can be clinically diagnosed as azoospermia, oligozoospermia, asthenozoospermia, or teratozoospermia (Jiao et al., 2021). However, only ~4% infertile men obtain a clear genetic diagnosis and most of the genetic pathogenic causes have not been explored (Tüttelmann et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2016 in the introduction section.

claim: Only approximately 4% of infertile men obtain a clear genetic diagnosis.
source: However, only ~4% infertile men obtain a clear genetic diagnosis and most of the genetic pathogenic causes have not been explored (Tüttelmann et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tüttelmann et al., 2018.

claim: DNAH1, CFAP43, CFAP44, CFAP69, CFAP251, ARMC2, TTC21A, TTC29, CFAP58, CFAP91, DNAH8, CFAP47, DNAH10, DNAH17, and WDR63 have been suggested as MMAF-associated genes.
source: With the development of whole-exome sequencing (WES) technology, DNAH1, CFAP43, CFAP44, CFAP69, CFAP251, ARMC2, TTC21A, TTC29, CFAP58, CFAP91, DNAH8, CFAP47, DNAH10, DNAH17, and WDR63 Ben Khelifa et al., 2014; Coutton et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2018; He et al., 2020; Kherraf et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020a; Liu et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2021a; Martinez et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020 have been suggested as MMAF-associated genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Mutations in CFAP65, QRICH2, CEP78, CEP128, CFAP70, and AKAP3 have been reported in Chinese patients with MMAF.
source: Our groups have reported mutations in CFAP65, QRICH2, CEP78, CEP128, CFAP70, and AKAP3 in Chinese patients with MMAF (Jin et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022a; Zhang et al., 2022b; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies by the authors' groups.

claim: Pathogenic mutations in SUN5 and PMFBP1 have been identified in ASS patients.
source: However, in the clinic, only pathogenic mutations in SUN5 and PMFBP1 (Elkhatib et al., 2017; Shang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021b; Zhu et al., 2016 Liu et al., 2020b; Lu et al., 2021b; Sha et al., 2019) have been identified in a large cohort of ASS patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: CFAP52 is a member of the large WD40-repeat protein family.
source: CFAP52 (cilia and flagella associated protein 52, also named WDR16) is a member of the large WD40-repeat protein family.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the protein family classification of CFAP52.

claim: FAP52 and FAP45 are orthologues of CFAP52 and CFAP45 in Chlamydomonas.
source: FAP52 and FAP45 are orthologues of CFAP52 and CFAP45 in Chlamydomonas, and a lack of these proteins causes an instability of microtubules (Owa et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Owa et al., 2019.

claim: Lack of FAP52 and FAP45 causes instability of microtubules in Chlamydomonas.
source: FAP52 and FAP45 are orthologues of CFAP52 and CFAP45 in Chlamydomonas, and a lack of these proteins causes an instability of microtubules (Owa et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Owa et al., 2019.

claim: Detachment of the B-tubule from the A-tubule and shortened flagella are observed in Chlamydomonas when both FAP52 and FAP20 are absent.
source: Detachment of the B-tubule from the A-tubule and shortened flagella are observed in Chlamydomonas when both FAP52 and FAP20 are absent (Owa et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Owa et al., 2019.

claim: The wdr16/cfap52 gene knockdown in zebrafish causes hydrocephalus.
source: The wdr16/cfap52 gene knockdown in zebrafish causes hydrocephalus (Hirschner et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hirschner et al., 2007.

claim: CFAP52 mutations have been identified in individuals who presented situs inversus totalis.
source: In humans, CFAP52 mutations have been identified in individuals who presented situs inversus totalis (Dougherty et al., 2020; TaShma et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dougherty et al., 2020 and TaShma et al., 2015.

claim: The patient's semen showed reduced sperm motility and abnormal sperm morphology.
source: We analysed the semen parameters of the patient, which mainly manifested as reduced sperm motility and abnormal sperm morphology (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: The patient's spermatozoa showed multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF), including short, coiled, absent, and irregular-calibre flagella.
source: Compared to a normal control, many patient's spermatozoa showed multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF), including short, coiled, absent, and irregular-calibre flagella (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: A high percentage of sperm decapitation was identified in the patient's semen.
source: Intriguingly, a high percentage of sperm decapitation was identified in the patient's semen (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Proximal centrioles were incomplete or invisible and some segmented columns were defective in the connecting piece of the patient's spermatozoa.
source: Despite the presence of basal plate (Bp), proximal centrioles (PCs) were incomplete or invisible and some segmented columns (Sc) were defective in the connecting piece of the patient's spermatozoa (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Disorganized or missing central pairs of microtubules were observed in the flagellar axoneme of the patient.
source: Furthermore, disorganized or missing central pairs of microtubules (CPs) were observed in the flagellar axoneme of the patient. Outer dense fibers (ODFs) and doublet microtubules (DMTs) were also partially lacking or disordered (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Outer dense fibers and doublet microtubules were partially lacking or disordered in the patient's spermatozoa.
source: Outer dense fibers (ODFs) and doublet microtubules (DMTs) were also partially lacking or disordered (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Compound heterozygous mutations c.203G>T and c.1128G>A in CFAP52 were identified in the patient.
source: The missense variant c.203G>T (p.S68I) and nonsense variant c.1128G>A (p.W376*) in CFAP52 had an extremely low frequency in public databases, including ExAC Browser, gnomAD, and the 1000 genome Project (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by WES data and frequency analysis in Table 2.

claim: The compound heterozygous CFAP52 variants in the patient were recessively inherited from their heterozygous parents.
source: Sanger sequencing of all the available family members confirmed that the compound heterozygous CFAP52 variants in the patient were recessively inherited from their heterozygous parents (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The affected sites of the CFAP52 variants were highly conserved among various species, including human, mouse, and rat.
source: Notably, the affected sites of the variants were highly conserved among various species, including human, mouse, and rat (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by conservation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The nonsense mutation c.1128G>A/p.W376* results in absence of CFAP52 protein expression.
source: Western blotting analysis showed that CFAP52 expression in the cells transfected with the CFAP52c.1128G>A plasmid was not detectable (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The c.203G>T variant was predicted to affect the splice site.
source: The c.203G>T variant was predicted to affect the splice site by the SPIDEX and SpliceAI tools (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational prediction tools as shown in Table 2.

claim: The splicing variant c.203G>T resulted in a deletion of exon 2 in the CFAP52 transcript.
source: Sanger sequencing further indicated that the splicing variant resulted in a deletion of exon 2 in the CFAP52 transcript (Figure 3C, D), which generated a frameshift variant p.D24Vfs*5 of CFAP52.
evidence: The claim is supported by minigene assay and Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: HEK293T cells transfected with the CFAP52c.203G>T plasmid did not express CFAP52 protein.
source: Western blotting results showed that HEK293T cells transfected with the CFAP52c.203G>T plasmid did not express CFAP52 protein (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CFAP52 was localized at both HTCA and full-length flagella in normal control spermatozoa.
source: By immunofluorescence staining of spermatozoa, we found that CFAP52 was localized at both HTCA and full-length flagella from the normal control; in contrast, CFAP52 signals were barely detected in the patient's spermatozoa (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CFAP52 signals were barely detected in the patient's spermatozoa.
source: By immunofluorescence staining of spermatozoa, we found that CFAP52 was localized at both HTCA and full-length flagella from the normal control; in contrast, CFAP52 signals were barely detected in the patient's spermatozoa (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Mouse CFAP52 was highly expressed in testes.
source: Mouse CFAP52 was highly expressed in testes and localized to the manchette (contributing to the formation of the HTCA and the sperm tail) of spermatids and the full-length sperm flagellum (including the HTCA; Tapia Contreras and Hoyer-Fender, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tapia Contreras and Hoyer-Fender, 2020.

claim: Mouse CFAP52 localized to the manchette of spermatids and the full-length sperm flagellum.
source: Mouse CFAP52 was highly expressed in testes and localized to the manchette (contributing to the formation of the HTCA and the sperm tail) of spermatids and the full-length sperm flagellum (including the HTCA; Tapia Contreras and Hoyer-Fender, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tapia Contreras and Hoyer-Fender, 2020.

claim: Cfap52-knockout mice were constructed by applying CRISPR/Cas9 technology that targeted exons 2 and 3 of the Cfap52-201 transcript.
source: To explore the physiological roles of CFAP52, we constructed Cfap52-knockout (KO) mice by applying CRISPR/Cas9 technology that targeted exons 2 and 3 of the Cfap52-201 transcript (ENSMUST00000021287.11; Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the knockout strategy shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The CFAP52 protein was completely absent in the Cfap52-KO testes compared with the WT testes.
source: The CFAP52 protein was completely absent in the Cfap52-KO testes compared with the WT testes (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cfap52-KO mice suffered from hydrocephalus.
source: Cfap52-KO mice suffered from hydrocephalus; the ependymal cilia was sparse under SEM observation and disrupted axonemal structures were identified by TEM analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEM and TEM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ependymal cilia was sparse in Cfap52-KO mice.
source: Cfap52-KO mice suffered from hydrocephalus; the ependymal cilia was sparse under SEM observation and disrupted axonemal structures were identified by TEM analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Disrupted axonemal structures were identified in ependymal cilia of Cfap52-KO mice.
source: Cfap52-KO mice suffered from hydrocephalus; the ependymal cilia was sparse under SEM observation and disrupted axonemal structures were identified by TEM analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: No obvious abnormalities of tracheal cilia were identified in Cfap52-KO mice.
source: However, no obvious abnormalities of tracheal cilia were identified by SEM and TEM analyses (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEM and TEM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cfap52-KO male mice were completely sterile.
source: Although Cfap52-KO male mice were able to mate normally with females, they were completely sterile because no pups were born using Cfap52-KO males (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by fertility test data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: Spermatozoa from Cfap52-KO mice had reduced sperm counts compared with WT mice.
source: Compared with spermatozoa from WT mice, spermatozoa from Cfap52-KO mice were not only small in quantity but also had poor motility (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by sperm count data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Spermatozoa from Cfap52-KO mice had poor motility compared with WT mice.
source: Compared with spermatozoa from WT mice, spermatozoa from Cfap52-KO mice were not only small in quantity but also had poor motility (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Cfap52-KO mice produced headless spermatozoa as well as spermatozoa with abnormal head-tail connections and aberrant tails.
source: Papanicolaou staining of spermatozoa indicated that Cfap52-KO mice produced headless spermatozoa as well as spermatozoa with abnormal head-tail connections and aberrant tails (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by Papanicolaou staining data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Decapitated spermatozoa accounted for approximately 40% of the total spermatozoa in Cfap52-KO mice.
source: Quantitative analyses showed that the decapitated spermatozoa, abnormal head-tail connecting spermatozoa, and spermatozoa with deformed flagella accounted for approximately 40%, 25%, and 30% of the total spermatozoa in Cfap52-KO mice, respectively (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Abnormal head-tail connecting spermatozoa accounted for approximately 25% of the total spermatozoa in Cfap52-KO mice.
source: Quantitative analyses showed that the decapitated spermatozoa, abnormal head-tail connecting spermatozoa, and spermatozoa with deformed flagella accounted for approximately 40%, 25%, and 30% of the total spermatozoa in Cfap52-KO mice, respectively (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Spermatozoa with deformed flagella accounted for approximately 30% of the total spermatozoa in Cfap52-KO mice.
source: Quantitative analyses showed that the decapitated spermatozoa, abnormal head-tail connecting spermatozoa, and spermatozoa with deformed flagella accounted for approximately 40%, 25%, and 30% of the total spermatozoa in Cfap52-KO mice, respectively (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: An enlarged gap between the nuclear envelope and axoneme was identified in Cfap52-KO spermatids.
source: In details, an enlarged gap between the nuclear envelope and axoneme (type 1, the second row) as well as ectopically localized mitochondria and vacuoles in the connecting piece (type 2, the third row) were often identified in Cfap52-KO spermatids, indicating hypoplasia and/or instability of the connecting piece.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ectopically localized mitochondria and vacuoles in the connecting piece were identified in Cfap52-KO spermatids.
source: In details, an enlarged gap between the nuclear envelope and axoneme (type 1, the second row) as well as ectopically localized mitochondria and vacuoles in the connecting piece (type 2, the third row) were often identified in Cfap52-KO spermatids, indicating hypoplasia and/or instability of the connecting piece.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The developing flagella was often misaligned with the nuclei in Cfap52-KO spermatids.
source: Due to a deficiency of connecting piece formation, the developing flagella was often misaligned with the nuclei (type 3, the fourth row).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The percentage of spermatids with ultra-structural defects of connecting piece in Cfap52-KO mice was significantly greater than that in WT mice.
source: Statistical analysis revealed that the percentage of spermatids (step 8~12) with ultra-structural defects of connecting piece in Cfap52-KO mice was significantly greater than that in WT mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Spermatozoa of Cfap52-KO mice displayed a disordered axoneme and accessory structures in the mid-piece.
source: In the mid-piece, WT spermatozoa have a well-defined MS, ODFs and the inside typical '9+2' axoneme, whereas spermatozoa of Cfap52-KO mice displayed a disordered axoneme and accessory structures (Figure 5D, the first row).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Axoneme and ODFs were partially lost in the principle piece of spermatozoa from Cfap52-KO mice.
source: In the principle piece, axoneme and ODFs were partially lost in spermatozoa of Cfap52-KO mice (Figure 5D, the second row).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The CP and DMTs were absent and disordered in the end-piece of spermatozoa from Cfap52-KO mice.
source: The CP and DMTs were also absent and disordered in the end-piece of spermatozoa from Cfap52-KO mice (Figure 5D, the third row).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: SPATA6 expression was significantly attenuated in the testis protein lysates of Cfap52-KO mice compared with WT mice.
source: The expression of most ASS-associated factors was unaltered except for SPATA6 and HOOK1 (Figure 6A). SPATA6 expression was significantly attenuated in the testis protein lysates of Cfap52-KO mice compared with WT mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: SPATA6 signals were barely detectable in the spermatozoa of the CFAP52-mutant patient.
source: SPATA6 signals were barely detectable in the spermatozoa of the CFAP52-mutant patient (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The degradation rate of SPATA6 was slowed by the presence of CFAP52.
source: The degradation rate of SPATA6 was obviously slowed by the presence of the cofactor CFAP52 (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: CFAP52 is critical for the expression of its interacting partner SPATA6.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that CFAP52 is critical for the expression of its interacting partner SPATA6, which may be the mechanism underlying the ASS phenotype in CFAP52-deficient mice and humans.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing CFAP52-SPATA6 interaction and SPATA6 stability regulation.

claim: The expression of components of MIPs (CFAP45 and ENKUR) was significantly reduced in sperm protein lysates of Cfap52-KO mice compared with WT mice.
source: By western blotting, we found that the expression of components of MIPs (CFAP45 and ENKUR) and radial spokes (RSPH3 and RSPH9) was significantly reduced in sperm protein lysates of Cfap52-KO mice compared with WT mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The expression of radial spoke components (RSPH3 and RSPH9) was significantly reduced in sperm protein lysates of Cfap52-KO mice compared with WT mice.
source: By western blotting, we found that the expression of components of MIPs (CFAP45 and ENKUR) and radial spokes (RSPH3 and RSPH9) was significantly reduced in sperm protein lysates of Cfap52-KO mice compared with WT mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The expression signals of CFAP45 were almost absent in the sperm flagella from the CFAP52-mutant patient.
source: By immunofluorescence staining, we further showed that the expression signals of CFAP45 and RSPH9 were almost absent in the sperm flagella from the CFAP52-mutant patient (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The expression signals of RSPH9 were almost absent in the sperm flagella from the CFAP52-mutant patient.
source: By immunofluorescence staining, we further showed that the expression signals of CFAP45 and RSPH9 were almost absent in the sperm flagella from the CFAP52-mutant patient (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Twenty oocytes were fertilized from 21 mature oocytes microinjected with the patient's sperm (fertilization rate 95.2%).
source: Then, 21 mature oocytes were microinjected, and 20 oocytes were ultimately fertilized (two-pronuclear/injected oocytes = 95.2%).
evidence: The claim is supported by ICSI outcome data presented in the text and Table 3.

claim: All 20 embryos from the patient's ICSI reached the cleavage stage and available D3 stage.
source: All 20 embryos reached the cleavage stage and further reached the available D3 stage.
evidence: The claim is supported by ICSI outcome data presented in the text and Table 3.

claim: The couple gave birth to a healthy newborn after one 4AA blastocyst was transplanted.
source: Finally, the couple gave birth to a healthy newborn after one 4AA blastocyst was transplanted (Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ICSI outcome data presented in the text and Table 3.

claim: Two-cell embryos and blastocysts were successfully obtained upon ICSI using the spermatozoa from Cfap52-KO mice.
source: Two-cell embryos and blastocyst were successfully obtained upon ICSI using the spermatozoa from Cfap52-KO mice, showing a similar efficiency with the control group (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ICSI data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: ICSI using spermatozoa from Cfap52-KO mice showed similar efficiency with the control group.
source: Two-cell embryos and blastocyst were successfully obtained upon ICSI using the spermatozoa from Cfap52-KO mice, showing a similar efficiency with the control group (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ICSI data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: ICSI could serve as a promising treatment for infertile men with CFAP52 variants.
source: Overall, our data suggest that ICSI could serve as a promising treatment for infertile men with CFAP52 variants.
evidence: The claim is based on the successful ICSI outcomes in both the patient and Cfap52-KO mice.

claim: CFAP52 is expected to be developed as a novel target for the genetic diagnosis of asthenoteratospermia.
source: Our findings help improve the understanding of the formation of head-tail connecting pieces and flagella as well as the genetic causes of male infertility. CFAP52 is expected to be developed as a novel target for the genetic diagnosis of asthenoteratospermia.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about future clinical applications of the research findings.

claim: CFAP52 interacts with SPATA6 and is essential for its stability.
source: CFAP52 interacts with a head-tail coupling regulator SPATA6 and is essential for its stability.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP and protein stability assay data.

claim: Expression of microtubule inner proteins was reduced after CFAP52 deficiency.
source: Expression of microtubule inner proteins and radial spoke proteins were reduced after the CFAP52 deficiency.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Expression of radial spoke proteins was reduced after CFAP52 deficiency.
source: Expression of microtubule inner proteins and radial spoke proteins were reduced after the CFAP52 deficiency.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting and immunofluorescence data.

claim: CFAP52-associated male infertility in humans and mice could be overcome by intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI).
source: Moreover, CFAP52-associated male infertility in humans and mice could be overcome by intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI).
evidence: The claim is supported by ICSI outcome data in both the patient and Cfap52-KO mice.

claim: CFAP52 plays a prominent role in sperm development.
source: The study reveals a prominent role for CFAP52 in sperm development, suggesting that CFAP52 might be a novel diagnostic target for male infertility with defects of sperm head-tail connection and flagella development
evidence: The claim is based on the comprehensive experimental data showing CFAP52's role in sperm development.

claim: CFAP52 might be a novel diagnostic target for male infertility with defects of sperm head-tail connection and flagella development.
source: The study reveals a prominent role for CFAP52 in sperm development, suggesting that CFAP52 might be a novel diagnostic target for male infertility with defects of sperm head-tail connection and flagella development
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about future clinical applications of the research findings.

claim: Cfap52-knockout mice resembled the human infertile phenotype, showing a mixed acephalic spermatozoa syndrome (ASS) and multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF) phenotype.
source: Cfap52-knockout mice resembled the human infertile phenotype, showing a mixed acephalic spermatozoa syndrome (ASS) and multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF) phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis data comparing Cfap52-KO mice and the patient.

claim: Ultrastructural analyses revealed a failure of connecting piece formation in Cfap52-KO mice.
source: The ultrastructural analyses further revealed a failure of connecting piece formation and a serious disorder of '9+2' axoneme structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Ultrastructural analyses revealed a serious disorder of '9+2' axoneme structure in Cfap52-KO mice.
source: The ultrastructural analyses further revealed a failure of connecting piece formation and a serious disorder of '9+2' axoneme structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5.

claim: SPATA6 encodes a protein required for the formation of Sc and Cp.
source: SPATA6 encodes a protein required for the formation of Sc and Cp (two major structures of the sperm HTCA), and inactivation of SPATA6 in mice leads to acephalic spermatozoa and male sterility (Yuan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yuan et al., 2015.

claim: Inactivation of SPATA6 in mice leads to acephalic spermatozoa and male sterility.
source: SPATA6 encodes a protein required for the formation of Sc and Cp (two major structures of the sperm HTCA), and inactivation of SPATA6 in mice leads to acephalic spermatozoa and male sterility (Yuan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yuan et al., 2015.

claim: FLAG-tagged CFAP52 interacted with Myc-tagged CFAP20, PACRG, DNAI2, ODAD1, ODAD3, RSPH1, and RSPH3 in HEK293T cells.
source: Using co-IP assays in HEK293T cells, we identified novel axonemal interactors of CFAP52, including components of MIPs (CFAP20 and PACRG), radial spokes (RSPH1 and RSPH3), and outer dynein arms and their docking complexes (DNAI2, ODAD1, and ODAD3; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: CFAP52 did not interact with components of inner dynein arm (DNALI1), dynein regulatory complexes (DRC2 and DRC4), or central apparatus (SPAG6).
source: CFAP52 did not interact with components of inner dynein arm (DNALI1), dynein regulatory complexes (DRC2 and DRC4), or central apparatus (SPAG6; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The protein levels of components of outer dynein arms (DNAI1 and DNAI2) were not altered in sperm samples of Cfap52-KO mice.
source: The protein levels of components of outer dynein arms (DNAI1 and DNAI2), inner dynein arms (DNAH7 and DNALI1), and dynein regulatory complexes (DRC2 and DRC4) were not altered in sperm samples of Cfap52-KO mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The protein levels of components of inner dynein arms (DNAH7 and DNALI1) were not altered in sperm samples of Cfap52-KO mice.
source: The protein levels of components of outer dynein arms (DNAI1 and DNAI2), inner dynein arms (DNAH7 and DNALI1), and dynein regulatory complexes (DRC2 and DRC4) were not altered in sperm samples of Cfap52-KO mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The protein levels of dynein regulatory complex components (DRC2 and DRC4) were not altered in sperm samples of Cfap52-KO mice.
source: The protein levels of components of outer dynein arms (DNAI1 and DNAI2), inner dynein arms (DNAH7 and DNALI1), and dynein regulatory complexes (DRC2 and DRC4) were not altered in sperm samples of Cfap52-KO mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The expression of DNAI1 was not lost in the patient's sperm flagella.
source: As a control, the expression of DNAI1 and DRC3 was not lost in the patient's sperm flagella (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The expression of DRC3 was not lost in the patient's sperm flagella.
source: As a control, the expression of DNAI1 and DRC3 was not lost in the patient's sperm flagella (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: SUN5 staining at the connecting piece was not lost in spermatozoa from the CFAP52-mutant patient.
source: As a positive control, SUN5 staining at the connecting piece was not lost in spermatozoa from the CFAP52-mutant patient (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The testis size of Cfap52-KO mice was similar to that of WT mice.
source: The testis size, testis/body weight ratio, and serum levels of hormones (e.g. GnRH and testosterone) of Cfap52-KO mice was all similar with those of WT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological and measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The testis/body weight ratio of Cfap52-KO mice was similar to that of WT mice.
source: The testis size, testis/body weight ratio, and serum levels of hormones (e.g. GnRH and testosterone) of Cfap52-KO mice was all similar with those of WT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The serum levels of GnRH and testosterone of Cfap52-KO mice were similar to those of WT mice.
